American Local Elections Study · 2025

Bucks County

What county residents think about local government and what they want it to do.

Viewing Results From:

In 2025 the Local Politics Lab conducted a national survey of 2,346 adults, along with post-election surveys of 5,517 adults in 33 cities and counties holding local elections to capture how the public views important issues facing their community. We asked respondents about their perceptions of local services and their elected leaders, along with their views on a variety of topics including housing, policing, immigration, and election timing. Here we report findings from the 153 respondents from Bucks County, Pennsylvania.

Key Findings
24percentapprove of Sheriff Fred Harran’s performance
44percentrate the cost of housing in Bucks County as below average or poor
37percentsay people like them have a great deal or fair amount of say in local government
52percentsupport moving Bucks County’s local elections to even-numbered years

Approval of elected officials

Majorities approve of the performance of Governor Josh Shapiro and disapprove of the performance of President Donald Trump. More respondents disapprove than approve of the performance of Sheriff Fred Harran, but nearly half of respondents say they do not know enough to rate Harran’s performance. Similarly, 56 percent of respondents are not able to rate the performance of District Attorney Jennifer Schorn. This is consistent with research showing that the public has limited knowledge about many local elected officials, particularly prosecutors.1

For some elected leaders, being unknown may be a bigger problem than being unpopular. Across the country, a large share of respondents say they do not know enough to rate the performance of their local officials.

Grades for local services

When asked to grade different aspects of their local community, Bucks County respondents give the highest grades to local schools, with 46 percent calling them excellent or above average. Respondents give the cost of housing the lowest grade.

Across the country, local institutions like schools and policing tend to receive the highest grades from the public, while broader economic conditions, especially the cost of housing, receive the worst.

Attribution and accountability

Federal, state, and local government agencies share responsibility for setting policies and delivering services that affect quality of life in Bucks County. This division of responsibility can make it difficult for the public to correctly assign credit or blame to local officials for policy decisions they make.2 Across different levels of government, respondents identify Bucks County government as most responsible for roads. Respondents most often assign responsibility for police, zoning, crime, traffic, schools, and housing costs to city and town governments within the county.

Although local governments have considerable discretion over many public services, the public may struggle to attribute policy outcomes to local elected leaders.

Government spending and revenue

To gauge budget priorities, the survey asked whether local governments should spend more, less, or about the same amount in eleven areas. Roads draw the strongest support for increased spending, at 55 percent. The largest partisan divides are over healthcare spending: 75 percent of Democrats favor increased spending, compared with 37 percent of Republicans, a difference of 38 percentage points.

Support for increased spending is substantially higher than support for increasing sources of government revenue. Fees and fines (parking, traffic tickets) draw the most support for an increase at 18 percent, and 50 percent of Bucks County respondents want property taxes cut.

Most Americans want more spending by local governments on education, housing, and healthcare, but do not support raising taxes.

Crime and policing

Bucks County respondents are more likely to perceive that crime has increased nationally than in their own neighborhoods. Nineteen percent say crime increased in their neighborhood over the past year, while 54 percent say it increased in the country as a whole.

National debates over policing and public safety have changed substantially since 2020. Following the murder of George Floyd and nationwide protests, many state and local governments placed limits on police use-of-force and instituted new requirements concerning body cameras, officer certification, and misconduct reporting. Progressive prosecutors also sought to address concerns over mass incarceration at the local level by declining to prosecute nonviolent misdemeanors.3 In more recent years, concerns about violent crime, shoplifting, and public disorder have helped fuel backlash against some of these reforms. Some police reforms, including requirements that officers wear body cameras, receive broad support in Bucks County. Support is lower for reducing the size of the local police force or limiting the types of crimes that are prosecuted.

Questions about the federal role in public safety became especially prominent in 2025 as the Trump administration deployed the National Guard and other military personnel in several American cities, including Los Angeles and Washington D.C. While a majority of Bucks County respondents say that responsibility for crime and policing lies primarily with state and local government, they report notable support for these types of federal deployments. Forty-one percent of Bucks County respondents agree that the military should participate in fighting crime in American cities, and 46 percent support bringing federal troops to their own city or town to address crime.

Despite declines in the national crime rate, a majority of Americans say that crime across the country has increased. Far fewer say crime has increased in their own community.

Housing and land use

In many American cities roughly three-quarters of residentially zoned land is reserved for detached single-family homes, a restriction that limits where apartments can be built and that is widely linked to housing shortages and higher costs.4 Fifty-eight percent of Bucks County respondents favor allowing multifamily housing throughout their city or town rather than limiting it to areas that are already densely developed, which is similar to support among Americans as a whole (66 percent).

Rent regulation has returned to the political agenda in a number of places, with attempts to freeze rents or otherwise limit rent increases in New York City, Massachusetts, and California.5 Perhaps due in part to the low grades Bucks County receives for the local cost of housing, 74 percent of Bucks County respondents favor limiting how much landlords can raise rent each year.

Transportation

Local transportation policy often involves tradeoffs among drivers, transit riders, pedestrians, and cyclists. Sixty-three percent of Bucks County respondents support the installation of new bus-only lanes to improve bus reliability, even if they reduce the space dedicated to driving and parking. Seventy percent favor subsidizing transit for low-income riders. While some jurisdictions have reduced or eliminated minimum parking requirements,6 65 percent of respondents favor increasing parking requirements for new housing. Such requirements can increase construction costs, particularly when they require structured or underground parking, and may reinforce automobile-oriented development.

Most respondents say city governments should prioritize pedestrian safety over increasing speed limits.

Immigration enforcement

Immigration policy received considerable attention in 2025 as federal agents carried out far-reaching immigration raids at workplaces, courthouses, and homes across the United States. As part of this effort, the Trump administration has attempted to place substantial pressure on local governments to abandon existing policies that limit when local police may assist immigration authorities.

Large majorities in Bucks County express support for federal policies that would allow immigrants already living in the United States to remain and obtain legal status. Sixty-two percent favor letting people brought to the United States illegally as children stay and work here, 69 percent favor a path to citizenship for immigrants already in the country, and 44 percent favor building a wall on the border with Mexico.

At the local level, 50 percent of Bucks County respondents favor letting local law enforcement cooperate with federal immigration authorities to deport people who are in the country illegally, while 50 percent either oppose the policy or did not express an opinion.7

Majorities support pro-immigrant policies at the federal level, while views on local cooperation with immigration enforcement are more divided.

Elections and representation

Perceived influence over local decision-making is a core indicator of civic efficacy and institutional responsiveness. In Bucks County, 37 percent of respondents say people like them have a great deal or a fair amount of say in what their local government does.

Election timing can affect who participates in local elections, and consequently whose preferences are reflected in the electorate. Research finds that local elections like those in Bucks County, which are held separately from federal elections, generally attract lower turnout and produce less representative electorates.8 Fifty-two percent favor moving Bucks County’s local elections from odd-numbered to even-numbered years, which would place them on the same general-election calendar as federal elections.

Seventy-seven percent agree that what happens in Washington shapes how they think about local issues in Bucks County. This perception is consistent with research documenting the increasing influence of national politics on local and subnational political behavior.9

Methodology

This report presents results from the 2025 wave of the American Local Elections Study, a project of the Local Politics Lab at the Harvard Kennedy School directed by Justin de Benedictis-Kessner. Data were collected by PureSpectrum, an online opt-in panel provider, with quota sampling within each surveyed jurisdiction. Interviews were conducted online between November 6 and December 15, 2025, following the November 4, 2025 local elections. The target population for this report is adults living in Bucks County; 153 respondents completed the survey. Data are weighted to population estimates for the jurisdiction from the 2023 5-year American Community Survey based on age, race and ethnicity, educational attainment, and sex. The margin of error for the Bucks County sample is +/- 9.2 percentage points at 95 percent confidence.
